title: Backups are proven restorable and rollback returns the previous sha
description:
SPIDR child 2 of task-7683a432eb3f4e87b1eb0cbc6e3a55ff (architect-20a6d1eb, 2026-09-05). dependsOn child 1 task-6ec875f4dd5f4f2ab97e46f71bf57b2b for the probe that confirms a rollback actually recovered.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: (a) scheduled BACKUPS of the project store and, per environment with a database, `pg_dump` - written under `<project>/.moe-next/backups/...` with a sha256 and a retention of N; (b) `deployment.rollback {environment, toReceiptRef}` (human-only), redeploying the previous image/sha with an atomic replace and the same health probe, optionally restoring the database backup taken at that deploy. No UI - child 3.

EVERY BACKUP IS PROVEN RESTORABLE. The parent's DoD 2 is unusually strong and correct: a restore-to-temp check whose sha256 is recorded PER RECEIPT. A backup that has never been restored is a file with a hopeful name, and the moment you discover otherwise is the moment you need it. This is the row's central property.

THE BACKUP LOCATION ALREADY HAS A CONVENTION: apps/daemon/src/bootstrap/activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33 defines BACKUP_DIRECTORY '.moe-next' and BACKUP_LEAF 'backups'. Reuse it - a second backup location is a second place to search during an incident. The migrations row (task-78eedd8ebc2b43c581ac21ea28648a9a, a sibling parent's child) writes `pg_dump` backups to the same tree; coordinate on the layout rather than interleaving two schemes.

ROLLBACK RESOLVES THROUGH THE KEPT DEPLOY RECEIPT that task-04b3ce7e349743c2a156d32ee5550ba5 stores (a SIBLING parent's row - no dependsOn allowed). Build against the shape recorded there. ROLLBACK_IMAGE_MISSING is the case that matters: the receipt names an image that no longer exists locally, and the honest answer is a refusal, not a rebuild from source, which would produce a different image under the same sha.

RETENTION PRUNES, AND THE RECEIPT SAYS WHAT IT PRUNED. Silent deletion of backups is how the one you needed disappears.
definitionOfDone: Scheduled backups write the project store and, per environment with a database, a `pg_dump`, under the EXISTING `.moe-next/backups` convention with a sha256 per backup. Assert the files exist and their recorded sha256 matches the bytes.

EVERY BACKUP IS PROVEN RESTORABLE: a restore-to-temp check runs per backup and its sha256 equality is RECORDED IN THE RECEIPT. Assert a real restore round trip, and assert that a backup which fails to restore is recorded as FAILED rather than kept as a good one - an unrestorable backup that reports success is worse than no backup, because it stops anyone looking for another.

RETENTION PRUNES TO N and the receipt LISTS THE PRUNED REFS. Assert the count after pruning and that the listed refs are the ones actually removed - silent deletion is how the backup you needed disappears.

`deployment.rollback` published HUMAN-ONLY and MCP-EXCLUDED with the full roster backfill and a bidirectional set-equality roster test. Rolling back a production environment is never an agent's decision.

The rollback offline test asserts the PREVIOUS IMAGE TAG is redeployed (resolved from the kept deploy receipt, not rebuilt from source - a rebuild under the same sha produces a different image) and that the DB restore is applied ONLY when requested. Assert the not-requested path leaves the database untouched.
ROLLBACK_RECEIPT_UNKNOWN, ROLLBACK_IMAGE_MISSING and BACKUP_FAILED each assert code + layer. ROLLBACK_IMAGE_MISSING refuses rather than rebuilding.
After a rollback the health probe from child 1 confirms recovery - assert the environment returns to UP through the real probe path, not through an internal flag.
Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`.
taskRails: A BACKUP THAT HAS NEVER BEEN RESTORED IS NOT A BACKUP. The restore-to-temp proof per receipt is this row's reason for existing.
NEVER REBUILD AN IMAGE TO SATISFY A ROLLBACK. A rebuild under the same sha is a different image; a missing image is ROLLBACK_IMAGE_MISSING.
RETENTION NAMES WHAT IT DELETED. Silent pruning loses the one you needed.
REUSE `.moe-next/backups` (activation-receipts-measure.ts:32-33) and coordinate the layout with the migrations row's pg_dump backups - one tree, one scheme.
`deployment.rollback` IS HUMAN-ONLY, and the DB restore happens ONLY when explicitly requested.

implementationPlan.description: MEASURE FIRST — HALF OF THIS ROW IS ALREADY BUILT, AND RE-IMPLEMENTING IT IS A SILENT DUPLICATE. NO EDITS. THIS ROW WAS NARROWED: it asked for backups, a NEW human-only command kind with a full roster backfill, AND the rollback effect. The command kind alone is a measured two-row roster job on this board, so three rows were cut and this one keeps the BACKUPS — DoD 1, 2, 3. The kind is task-37a50989 (contract) and task-b22462cf (daemon + fence); the effect is task-da60dc4b. DoD 4, 5, 6 and 7 of the text you are reading are THEIRS, not yours; where description and plan disagree, THE PLAN IS AUTHORITY. Its `dependsOn` on the probe row was also dropped — backups need no probe. (a) READ WHAT EXISTS BEFORE WRITING ANYTHING (rail 19, gap-claimed-present direction). `apps/daemon/src/bootstrap/activation-receipts-measure.ts` (273 lines) ALREADY: writes the store backup to `join(projectRoot, '.moe-next', 'backups')` as `<17-digit ms stamp>.sqlite` (:145-155); takes a REAL `node:sqlite` online backup through an injected `ports.backup`; computes a sha256 and records `ref = <destination>@sha256:<sha>` (:175-177); refuses to overwrite an existing destination as a check-then-act guard it documents as NOT mutual exclusion (:161-165); and defines `BACKUP_RETENTION = 5` with a `pruneBackups` that keeps the newest N (:179-200). So DoD-1's store half and DoD-3's pruning half largely EXIST. Confirm all of it at the tree, then say in the step note which clauses were already satisfied and which are genuinely new — a row that re-implements this would collide with the activation path that calls it. (b) WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING, and this is the row's real work: SCHEDULED backups (today's is activation-triggered), the per-environment `pg_dump`, THE RESTORE-TO-TEMP PROOF (DoD-2, and nothing today restores anything), and a pruning that NAMES WHAT IT DELETED — `pruneBackups` is documented "Housekeeping only" and swallows every failure silently (:193-198), which is the opposite of DoD-3's requirement. (c) NOTE THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES THE DESIGN: `pruneBackups` and `measureBackup` are private to a module the ACTIVATION path calls, and `activation-read.ts:7` documents that the read route never writes. Decide whether you extend that module or build a scheduled backup service beside it that REUSES its path convention and retention constant — and prefer the second unless you can show the first does not entangle activation with scheduling. Say which and why. (d) BASELINE (global rail 3), standalone foreground, quoting each count line: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test`. (e) `git status --porcelain -- apps/daemon/src` and note peer dirt.

THE RESTORE PROOF — THIS ROW'S REASON FOR EXISTING, AND THE ONE THING NOTHING TODAY DOES. NEW MODULE under `apps/daemon/src/backup/` plus its `.js` bridge. A BACKUP THAT HAS NEVER BEEN RESTORED IS A FILE WITH A HOPEFUL NAME, and the moment you discover otherwise is the moment you need it. Note precisely what today's sha256 does and does not prove: `measureBackup` hashes THE BACKUP FILE'S OWN BYTES, which proves the file is intact — it does NOT prove the file is a loadable database. A truncated-but-intact sqlite file, or a `pg_dump` that failed halfway and exited 0, both hash perfectly. THE PROOF IS A RESTORE INTO A TEMPORARY LOCATION, then a check that the restored artifact is genuinely usable — for the store, open it and read something; for a `pg_dump`, restore into a disposable database and confirm a table exists. `exit 0` is not proof, exactly as it is not for a migration tool. RECORD THE RESULT PER RECEIPT (DoD-2): the restore's own sha256 equality, and an explicit VERIFIED / FAILED disposition. A BACKUP THAT FAILS TO RESTORE IS RECORDED AS FAILED, NEVER KEPT AS A GOOD ONE — an unrestorable backup that reports success is worse than no backup, because it stops anyone looking for another. Make that its own arm in step 4. EVERYTHING THE PROOF CREATES IS RELEASED ON EVERY EXIT PATH INCLUDING THE THROWING ONE (epic rail 4): the temp directory, the restored copy, any disposable database — teardown in a `finally`, never after the assertions. A restore proof that leaks a temp database on failure would poison the very gate that runs it.

SCHEDULED BACKUPS, THE pg_dump LEG, AND PRUNING THAT NAMES ITS DEAD. New modules beside step 2's, reusing the LANDED convention rather than re-deriving it — `.moe-next/backups`, the 17-digit millisecond stamp, and `BACKUP_RETENTION` — because a second backup location is a second place to search during an incident (rail 4). (1) THE STORE BACKUP ALREADY HAS A WRITER; what is new is the SCHEDULE. Take the clock and the schedule as injected facts so the tests drive time rather than wait on it. (2) THE `pg_dump` LEG, per environment with a database. It is the one that spawns: bare executable under `shell: false` with an ARGV ARRAY — never a shell string, never a chain, and never a pipe (a piped run reports the wrong exit code and you have no shell to ask). COORDINATE THE LAYOUT with task-78eedd8e, which writes `pg_dump` backups to the same tree for the migrations path — one tree, one scheme, and if that row has landed, follow what it chose rather than interleaving a second naming. (3) PRUNING MUST NAME WHAT IT DELETED (DoD-3), and this is a BEHAVIOUR CHANGE rather than an addition: today's `pruneBackups` is "Housekeeping only", swallows a failed listing and a failed removal, and returns nothing. Silent deletion is how the backup you needed disappears. Return the pruned refs, record them on the receipt, and decide DELIBERATELY what a FAILED removal does — reporting it is defensible, ignoring it as today does is defensible for housekeeping, but a receipt that lists a ref as pruned when the file is still there is not. Say which you chose. If you extend the existing function rather than writing a new one, remember the activation path calls it and its current contract is documented as never affecting the measured receipt. (4) The receipt shape itself: if you add one, mirror `repository/publish-receipt-contracts.ts` — a versioned `moe-*-receipt/1` under an `internal.*` command kind, which needs NO roster backfill because `internal.*` kinds sit outside PAYLOAD_KEYS, the registry and the MCP roster entirely.

TESTS, WITH THE UNRESTORABLE-BACKUP ARM FIRST. New test files beside their modules. Every port injected; no test reaches a real database or a real filesystem outside a temp directory it owns and removes. (1) DoD-2's HARD HALF, and the arm that justifies the row: a backup that FAILS to restore is recorded FAILED, not kept as good. Plant a corrupt or truncated artifact whose FILE HASH IS PERFECTLY VALID — that is the case today's sha256 cannot see — and assert the disposition is FAILED and the receipt says so. An arm that only tests a healthy backup proves the happy path and leaves the property untested. (2) DoD-2's round trip: a real restore into a temp location, its sha256 equality recorded per receipt, and the temp artifacts gone afterwards — assert the cleanup by listing the directory, not by trusting the code. (3) DoD-1: the files exist under the EXISTING `.moe-next/backups` convention and each recorded sha256 matches the bytes on disk — recompute from the file rather than re-reading the value the writer recorded, which would be circular. (4) DoD-3: after pruning, the count is N and the receipt's listed refs are EXACTLY the files that disappeared — assert the set equality both ways (every listed ref is gone, every gone file is listed), because a receipt listing a subset passes a naive check while losing the record of the rest. (5) `BACKUP_FAILED` asserted with code AND layer, reusing an already-rostered layer literal — introduce no new `*_LAYER` constant. (6) THE SCHEDULE: assert it fires on the injected clock and that two runs in the same millisecond do not collide — the landed writer refuses a same-millisecond retry rather than overwriting, and that behaviour must survive.

DRILLS, GATES, SELF-REVIEW. (a) DRILLS. `git status --porcelain` the exact mutated paths FIRST. EVERY FILE THIS ROW CREATES IS NEW AND UNTRACKED, so `git diff` is BLIND to all of them — SHA256 against an out-of-tree backup (%TEMP%, suffixed by worker id), proved in a call SEPARATE from the restore. If you also edited the landed activation module, that path is TRACKED and takes an empty `git diff`; say which proof applies to which path. THREE DRILLS: (i) THE ROW'S CENTRAL DRILL — make the restore proof report VERIFIED without actually restoring (return early, keep the hash check) and confirm the corrupt-artifact arm from step 4 goes RED. If it stays green, the arm was testing the file hash, which today's code already does, and this row has added nothing. Quote the red. (ii) Make pruning delete without recording, and confirm the DoD-3 set-equality arm reds naming the unlisted ref. (iii) Make the temp restore skip its cleanup and confirm the arm that lists the directory reds — not the one that trusts a flag. (b) GATES — standalone foreground, one command per call, no pipes and no `;` chains, quoting each `Test Files N passed` count line: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`. Root `pnpm test` is NOT evidence for this row's daemon files — vitest.config.ts has no `apps/**` — so if you quote it, say what it covers. Attribute red by failing paths at HEAD minus the step-1 baseline, intersected with this row's owned paths. (c) ADVERSARIAL PASS on this diff only: a `pg_dump` that exits 0 having written nothing (the exact case the restore proof exists for — is it caught?); a backup taken while the store is being written; the restore proof running on a machine with no postgres (refusal, or silent skip — a skip here is the same failure class as the verifier's); disk full during a restore-to-temp; a retention of N with fewer than N backups; two scheduled runs overlapping; whether a `pg_dump` file could contain a credential and whether it is protected on disk. (d) COMPLETION RECORD must state: which DoD clauses were ALREADY SATISFIED by the landed activation backup and which were genuinely new — quoting the grep — so a grader does not read reuse as an omission; the failed-removal decision from step 3; the layout you agreed with task-78eedd8e for `pg_dump` files; drill (i) verbatim; and that DoD 4-7 of the original text belong to task-37a50989, task-b22462cf and task-da60dc4b, none of them touched here.

comments.content:
SPLIT FOUR WAYS, AND HALF THE REMAINING WORK IS ALREADY BUILT. architect-b63fabf3, 2026-09-05, HEAD f3b94eaa. Plan approved: 5 steps, 5 files, all new. Where description and plan disagree, THE PLAN IS AUTHORITY.

## Why it split

The row carried backups, a **new human-only command kind with "the full roster backfill and a bidirectional set-equality roster test"**, and the rollback effect. Measured: `deployment.rollback` = **zero hits** anywhere, while `deployment.deploy`/`deployment.set_target` already sit on the roster. So publishing it is the same shape its sibling just paid for — a 6-file contract slice (the roster line rotates the contract digest, four mirrors, two invisible to every gate but `pnpm --filter @moe/control-room test`) plus a ~6-file daemon slice. Neither fits with the other, and neither fits with a backup subsystem.

- **task-37a50989** — the contract roster + all four digest mirrors
- **task-b22462cf** — daemon wiring + the operator fence, `dependsOn` the contract row
- **task-da60dc4b** — the rollback **effect**, `dependsOn` the wiring + this row + the probe
- **this row** — backups only: DoD 1, 2, 3

I also **dropped this row's `dependsOn` on the probe row** (task-6ec875f4, PLANNING). Backups need no health probe — checked against all three remaining DoD items. It is claimable now rather than gated behind a PLANNING sibling.

## Half of DoD-1 and DoD-3 already exist

`activation-receipts-measure.ts` already writes the store backup to `.moe-next/backups/<17-digit ms stamp>.sqlite` through a real `node:sqlite` online backup, computes a **sha256**, records `<path>@sha256:<hash>`, refuses to overwrite an existing destination, and prunes to `BACKUP_RETENTION = 5`. A worker reading DoD-1 and DoD-3 cold would rebuild all of it — and collide with the activation path that calls it.

**What is genuinely new:** the *schedule* (today's is activation-triggered), the per-environment `pg_dump`, the restore proof, and a pruning that **names what it deleted** — today's is documented "Housekeeping only" and swallows every failure silently, which is the opposite of DoD-3.

## The existing sha256 is not the restore proof, and it looks like one

It hashes the backup **file's own bytes** — integrity, not loadability. **A truncated sqlite file and a `pg_dump` that failed halfway and exited 0 both hash perfectly.** That gap *is* this row.

So the test that matters plants a corrupt artifact whose **file hash is valid**, and drill (i) makes the proof report VERIFIED without actually restoring: if the arm stays green, it was testing the file hash — which today's code already does — and this row added nothing.

## Three smaller things

- **A healthy-only test proves the happy path.** DoD-2's hard half is that an unrestorable backup is recorded FAILED, not kept as good — a false green stops anyone looking for another copy.
- **Pruning that lists a subset** passes a naive check while losing the record of the rest. Assert set equality both ways.
- **Changing `pruneBackups`' contract touches activation** — its docblock promises the measured receipt survives a pruning failure. Decide deliberately; do not silently break that promise.

If a new receipt is wanted, `publish-receipt-contracts.ts` is the precedent: a versioned `moe-*-receipt/1` under an `internal.*` kind, which needs **no roster backfill** at all.

planningNotes.risks:
FIRST — RE-IMPLEMENTING WHAT EXISTS. The store backup, its sha256, the `.moe-next/backups` path, the stamp format and the retention constant are all LANDED and called by the activation path. A worker reading DoD-1 and DoD-3 cold will rebuild them. Step 1 exists to stop that, and the completion record must say which clauses were already satisfied so a grader does not read reuse as an omission.

SECOND — THE EXISTING sha256 IS NOT THE RESTORE PROOF, and it looks like one. It hashes the backup file's own bytes: a truncated sqlite database and a `pg_dump` that failed halfway and exited 0 both hash perfectly. Drill (i) makes the proof report VERIFIED without restoring and requires the corrupt-artifact arm to red — if it stays green, the arm is testing the file hash and this row added nothing.

THIRD — A HEALTHY-ONLY TEST PROVES THE HAPPY PATH. DoD-2's hard half is that an unrestorable backup is recorded FAILED, not kept as good, because a false green stops anyone looking for another copy. The corrupt artifact must have a VALID file hash, or the arm is testing the wrong thing.

FOURTH — PRUNING THAT LISTS A SUBSET passes a naive check while losing the record of the rest. Assert set equality BOTH ways: every listed ref is gone, every gone file is listed.

FIFTH — CHANGING `pruneBackups`' CONTRACT TOUCHES ACTIVATION. Its docblock promises the measured receipt is unaffected by a pruning failure. Decide deliberately what a failed removal does now, and do not silently break that promise for the activation path.
